subject: Chemistry
topic: Atomic models, ions, isotopes and electron arrangements
scope: Original partial support for AQA GCSE Chemistry 8462 points 4.1.1.3-7, checked 2026-10-19. Covers the nuclear model and first-twenty-element shell representations, not the whole periodic table or a full quantum description. Independent subject review remains pending.
prerequisites: Read element symbols and whole-number particle counts.
Calculate weighted means and convert simple percentages.
objectives: Use proton number, mass number and ion charge to count particles.
Distinguish an isotope from an ion and a relative atomic mass from a mass number.
Explain why scattering evidence supports a compact nuclear model.
Represent electron arrangements for selected first-twenty-element atoms.

notes.heading: A model is an explanation constrained by evidence
paragraphs: An atomic model represents features that help us explain observations; it is not a magnified photograph. Early indivisible-sphere pictures could not account for evidence that atoms contain negatively charged electrons. A model with electrons embedded in distributed positive charge addressed electrical neutrality but made different scattering predictions from a model with charge concentrated in a tiny nucleus. The useful question is not simply which model came later, but which observations a model can and cannot explain.

In the alpha-particle scattering account used here, most particles pass through the thin foil with little deflection, while a very small fraction are strongly deflected. The combination supports a mostly empty atomic volume with positive charge and much of the mass concentrated in a compact centre. A few large deflections are especially informative: a model must explain those as well as the common straight paths. The experiment did not directly show electron shells, and it did not by itself establish the neutron. Those features required additional evidence.

notes.heading: Particle bookkeeping and electrical charge
paragraphs: A proton has relative charge +1 and a neutron has charge 0. An electron has relative charge −1. Protons and neutrons each have relative mass approximately 1, while an electron is much lighter. Proton number Z identifies the element. If a species contains 12 protons, it is magnesium regardless of how many electrons it has. Changing the proton number changes the element; removing an electron does not. Chemical ion formation rearranges electrons without changing the nucleus in this model.

For a neutral atom, the electron count equals Z because the charges cancel. For an ion with signed charge q measured in elementary-charge units, electron count is Z−q. A 2+ ion therefore has two fewer electrons than protons; a 1− ion has one more. Write the sign before substituting: subtracting a negative charge adds an electron. A useful check is to reconstruct net charge as protons minus electrons. Never subtract the charge from the neutron count, because neutrons carry no electrical charge.

notes.heading: Isotopes, mass numbers and physical scale
paragraphs: Mass number A counts the protons and neutrons in one nucleus, so neutron count is A−Z. Isotopes share Z but differ in neutron count. For example, a hypothetical sample of magnesium-24 and magnesium-26 contains nuclei with the same 12 protons but different neutron totals. The element identity is unchanged. An isotope can also be ionised: isotope identity and ion charge answer different questions, so a species can differ from another in both neutrons and electrons.

Atomic dimensions need powers of ten rather than ordinary whole-number drawings. A radius of 0.10 nm equals 1.0×10⁻¹⁰ m because nano means one billionth. The nucleus is vastly smaller than the atom, and ordinary shell sketches are not to scale. Most atomic mass is associated with the nucleus even though the nucleus occupies very little volume. Keep radius comparisons separate from volume comparisons: multiplying a radius by a factor multiplies the volume of a similar sphere by the cube of that factor. No exact universal nuclear radius is assumed here.

notes.heading: Why relative atomic mass can be non-integer
paragraphs: Relative atomic mass describes an abundance-weighted mean on the relative atomic-mass scale, not the nucleon count of a particular atom. In classroom isotope calculations, the supplied isotope masses are often approximated by integer mass numbers. If 60% of a fictional sample has mass 10 and 40% has mass 11, the mean is 0.60×10+0.40×11=10.4. There is no need to invent an atom with 10.4 nucleons. The average describes a collection.

First check that abundances use a consistent basis and sum to the full sample. With percentages, divide the weighted sum by 100; with counts, divide by the total count. The result must lie between the smallest and largest isotope masses, and it should be closer to the more abundant mass. An unweighted mean is appropriate only for equal abundances. Relative atomic mass has no unit; a sample mass in grams is a different quantity. Real high-precision isotope masses are not always exactly the mass numbers, so retain supplied data and avoid claiming unnecessary precision.

notes.heading: Electron shells as a bounded school representation
paragraphs: For the selected ground-state atoms among the first twenty elements, electron arrangements can be written as numbers in successive occupied shells. Sodium has 11 electrons arranged 2,8,1; chlorine has 17 arranged 2,8,7; calcium has 20 arranged 2,8,8,2. Count the entries to check the total. A drawing uses a nucleus and labelled shells with the same electron numbers. The drawn circles are a representation of energy levels, not literal tracks measured in the scattering experiment.

An ion requires a fresh electron count. Sodium forming Na⁺ loses its outer electron and is represented as 2,8. Chlorine forming Cl⁻ gains an electron and is represented as 2,8,8. Neither process changes the proton number. The simple first-twenty pattern must not be extended into a claim that every shell can hold only eight electrons. Later chemistry uses subshells and orbitals to account for more complicated configurations. This lesson uses the bounded school model because it supports the named task, while keeping that limitation explicit.

notes.heading: A reliable solution and revision routine
paragraphs: Start a particle-count question by listing the information separately: element or Z, isotope mass number A, and charge q. Then calculate protons Z, neutrons A−Z, and electrons Z−q. Check that counts are non-negative whole numbers and that protons minus electrons reproduces the charge. If a question supplies only a periodic-table relative atomic mass, do not silently round it and pretend that a unique isotope was specified. Additional isotope information may be needed to determine the neutron count.

For an explanation, connect each statement to what it supports. A mostly empty volume explains the frequent low-deflection observations; concentrated positive charge explains rare large deflections. For an isotope average, show weights and a sensible-range check. For a shell diagram, show the correct electron total and identify whether the species is neutral. A complete revision session alternates these skills instead of memorising only definitions. Remaining work includes broader element recall, periodic trends and more diagram construction; successful answers here do not establish completion of the whole atomic-structure unit.

notes.heading: Inferring an ion from particle counts
paragraphs: Atomic number identifies an element through its proton count. An ion retains that identity when electrons are transferred; changing protons would change the element. Work from the signed difference between protons and electrons to find the charge, and use protons plus neutrons for the mass number. These are counts for one specified isotope, not a naturally occurring weighted relative atomic mass. A shell drawing can represent the electron count but does not replace the particle accounting. For the first twenty elements, the simplified shell model is useful within its school-level scope. It should not be used to infer that every atom fills shells according to an unrestricted 2,8,8 pattern.

notes.heading: Use particle counts and mixture fractions separately
paragraphs: Particle bookkeeping applies to a single atom or ion; isotope averaging applies to a collection. The atomic number fixes the element, the mass number counts protons plus neutrons, and the ionic charge compares protons with electrons. Isotopes of an element can have different neutron counts but the same number of protons. For a mixture of two isotope masses, the average must lie between those masses and move toward the more abundant one. A fractional mean does not mean that an individual nucleus contains a fractional neutron.

workedExamples.prompt: An ion has Z=13, A=27 and charge 3+. Find its particle counts.
A fictional element has 80 atoms of isotope mass 20 and 20 atoms of isotope mass 22. Find its mean relative mass.
steps: Check that the mean lies between 20 and 22, closer to 20.

workedExamples.prompt: Compare neutral chlorine-35 and chloride-35, both with Z=17.
steps: Both nuclei contain 17 protons and 35−17=18 neutrons.
The neutral atom has 17 electrons; the 1− ion has 18.
Write the school shell arrangements as 2,8,7 and 2,8,8.
workedExamples.answer: Ion formation changes electrons, not isotope identity.

workedExamples.prompt: Convert an atomic radius of 0.12 nm into metres.
steps: Multiply 0.12 by 10⁻⁹ and put it in standard form.

workedExamples.prompt: Why does a small minority of strongly deflected alpha particles matter?
steps: A satisfactory model must account for rare observations as well as common ones.
Large deflections support concentrated charge rather than only a diffuse positive background.
workedExamples.answer: They discriminate between competing charge-distribution models; they do not establish electron shells by themselves.

workedExamples.prompt: A particle has 13 protons, 14 neutrons and 10 electrons. Give its atomic number, mass number and charge, explaining each.
steps: Mass number counts protons and neutrons: 13 + 14 = 27.
There are three more protons than electrons, giving a charge of 3+.

misconceptions.claim: An ion is a different element because its charge changed.
misconceptions.correction: The element is fixed by proton number, not electron count.

misconceptions.claim: An isotope mean of 24.5 means each nucleus contains half a neutron.
misconceptions.correction: The mean describes abundances across a sample, not the particle count in one nucleus.

misconceptions.claim: The first-twenty shell pattern proves every shell holds at most eight electrons.
misconceptions.correction: It is a bounded representation, not a universal shell-capacity rule.

flashcards.front: Which particle count fixes element identity?
How many electrons does a neutral atom have?
flashcards.back: The same number as its protons.

flashcards.front: How do you obtain signed ion charge from particle counts?
flashcards.back: Protons minus electrons, in elementary-charge units.

flashcards.front: What is the neutron count for mass number A and proton number Z?
What differs between isotopes of one element?
flashcards.back: Neutron count; proton number remains fixed.

flashcards.front: What changes when an atom forms an ion through ordinary electron transfer?
Why can relative atomic mass be non-integer?
flashcards.back: It is an abundance-weighted mean of isotope masses.

flashcards.front: What is wrong with averaging isotope masses without weights?
flashcards.back: It assumes equal abundance, which may not match the sample.

flashcards.front: What does mostly low-deflection alpha scattering support?
flashcards.back: Most atomic volume contains no concentrated obstacle to the particles.

flashcards.front: What do rare strong alpha deflections support?
flashcards.back: Positive charge concentrated in a small region.

flashcards.front: What is the first-twenty shell representation of Cl⁻?
What conversion connects nanometres to metres?
Does forming an ion by electron transfer change its mass number?
flashcards.back: No. Mass number counts protons and neutrons, which are unchanged by electron transfer.

flashcards.front: How is ionic charge found from particle counts?
flashcards.back: Subtract the electron count from the proton count, expressing the result as a signed charge in elementary-charge units.

questions.prompt: Which change alone turns a neutral sodium atom into Na⁺?
solution: Proton count must stay fixed for the element to remain sodium.
Removing a negative charge gives net charge +1.

questions.prompt: Sulfur-34 has Z=16. How many neutrons are in its nucleus?
solution: Mass number counts protons plus neutrons.
Subtract 16 from 34.

questions.prompt: Explain why magnesium-24 and magnesium-26 are the same element.
questions.answer: Both have 12 protons; their neutron counts differ.
solution: Identify proton number as the element criterion.
Distinguish isotope variation in neutrons.

questions.prompt: A fictional sample contains 70% isotope mass 10 and 30% isotope mass 11. Calculate the mean relative atomic mass.
solution: Weight the masses by 0.70 and 0.30.
Add 7.0 and 3.3; check the answer lies between 10 and 11.

questions.prompt: Explain how mostly straight alpha paths and rare large deflections support different features of the nuclear model. State one conclusion this experiment alone does not establish.
questions.answer: Mostly straight paths support a largely empty volume; rare large deflections support concentrated positive charge in a compact nucleus. The experiment alone does not establish the electron-shell arrangements.
solution: Separate the two observations.
Connect each to its model feature.
Avoid inferring electron-shell arrangements from this experiment alone.
markingPoints: Identify a limit of this evidence.

questions.prompt: Calcium has Z=20. How many electrons does Ca²⁺ contain?
solution: The neutral atom has 20 electrons.
A 2+ charge means two electrons have been lost.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes a sample with relative atomic mass 35.5?
options: The abundance-weighted mean can be 35.5 even though each mass number is an integer.
Every atom has half an electron.
The element must contain equal numbers of every possible isotope.
questions.answer: The abundance-weighted mean can be 35.5 even though each mass number is an integer.
solution: An average is not an individual particle count.
Different isotope abundances can produce a fractional mean.

questions.prompt: Write the school shell arrangements of a neutral sodium atom and Na⁺, with Z=11.
solution: Count 11 electrons for the neutral atom and 10 for the ion.
Fill the bounded shell representation and verify the totals.

questions.prompt: A learner uses the periodic-table value 24.3 to claim that every magnesium atom has 12.3 neutrons. Explain two errors.
questions.answer: A relative atomic mass is a weighted sample mean, not a mass number. Individual neutron counts are whole numbers and require the particular isotope's mass number.
solution: Identify the type of given value.
Explain the information required for A−Z.
State why a fractional neutron count is not the interpretation.

questions.prompt: For an ion with Z=8, A=18 and charge 2−, give all particle counts and check its charge.
solution: Use Z for protons and A−Z for neutrons.
Use Z−(−2) for electrons.
Reconstruct signed charge.

questions.prompt: A particle has 13 protons, 14 neutrons and 10 electrons. Give its atomic number, mass number and charge, explaining each.
solution: Atomic number equals the 13 protons.
Mass number counts protons and neutrons: 13 + 14 = 27.
There are three more protons than electrons, giving a charge of 3+.
markingPoints: Mass number counts protons and neutrons: 13 + 14 = 27.
There are three more protons than electrons, giving a charge of 3+.

questions.prompt: A learner says this particle became a 3+ ion by gaining three protons. Correct the explanation while preserving its element identity.
questions.answer: It lost three electrons from a neutral atom with 13 electrons; its proton count remains 13.
solution: The proton count defines the element.
A neutral atom with 13 protons has 13 electrons.
Removing three electrons leaves 10 and produces charge 3+ without changing the element.
markingPoints: The proton count defines the element.
A neutral atom with 13 protons has 13 electrons.
Removing three electrons leaves 10 and produces charge 3+ without changing the element.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical element has only isotopes of masses 20 and 22. Its mean isotope mass is 20.6. Find the percentage of the mass-22 isotope.
solution: Let f be the fraction of mass-22 atoms: 20(1-f)+22f=20.6.
Then 2f=0.6, so f=0.30.

questions.prompt: Particle X has 12 protons and 10 electrons; particle Y has 9 protons and 10 electrons. Give their charges and explain why the same electron count does not make them the same element.
questions.answer: X is 2+ and Y is 1−. Different proton counts identify different elements despite equal electron counts.
solution: Calculate each charge as protons minus electrons in elementary-charge units.
Use atomic number, not electron number, to determine element identity.

questions.prompt: An atom initially has 6 protons and 8 neutrons. In a hypothetical nuclear change, one neutron becomes a proton. Ignore the subsequent electron arrangement. State the new atomic number and mass number and whether element identity changes.
questions.answer: Atomic number 7, mass number 14; the element changes.
solution: The nucleus now contains 7 protons and 7 neutrons.
The total nucleon count is unchanged but the proton count changes.
markingPoints: Link changed proton count to changed element.

revisionChecklist: Separate isotope mass number from a sample's relative atomic mass.
Link scattering observations to distinct model claims.
Check shell totals and keep the model's scope explicit.
Explain the reasoning in “Read particle counts in three steps” and correct the linked error-analysis response without copying its solution.

diagrams.title: Read particle counts in three steps
diagrams.description: Read the labelled relationships to follow this worked application. Atomic number 13; mass number 27; charge 3+. This is an explanatory process diagram, not a scale drawing or a record of a learner attempt.

steps.label: Isotope
steps.detail: 13 protons plus 14 neutrons give mass number 27.

steps.label: Ion
steps.detail: 13 positive charges and 10 negative charges give net charge 3+.
